rendered:
The documents don't answer this directly. None of them tests a sodium-ion electrolyte in a lithium-ion battery, and none says whether it would work.

What they do show is that the sodium-ion work uses sodium-specific electrolytes. A study uses NaPF6 in diglyme, chosen for its stability against sodium metal and tendency to form stable SEI layers for sodium-based chemistries[1]. Another uses NaPF6 salts in tetraglyme: coin cells were assembled using NaPF6 salts dissolved in tetraglyme as electrolyte[2].

The lithium-ion documents use lithium salts in carbonate solvents. The standard LIB electrolyte is described as Electrolyte systems in LIBs are typically made of a lithium salt, LiPF6, dissolved in a mixture of linear carbonate solvents[3]. Another uses The electrolyte used was 1.2 M LiPF6 in ethylene carbonate/ethylmethyl carbonate[4].

The sodium papers also note that sodium metal is less stable with carbonate electrolytes than lithium metal[5]. So the evidence points the other way: the sodium cells rely on glyme-based electrolytes chosen for sodium, and the lithium-ion cells use LiPF6 in carbonates. Whether a sodium salt could be used in a lithium-ion cell is not addressed in the documents provided, so it would need a separate test.
